### Summary  

**a. Verdict** – I have obtained a complete solution.  
For every integer \(n\ge 3\) the set of admissible numbers of sunny lines is  

\[
\boxed{\begin{cases}
\{0,1,3,4,\dots ,n\}, & n=4,\\[2mm]
\{0,1,3,\,n\},          & n=3,\\[2mm]
\{0,1,2,\dots ,n\},     & n\ge 5 .
\end{cases}}
\]

In words  

* for \(n=3\) the only possible values are \(k=0,1,3\);  
* for \(n=4\) the possible values are \(k=0,1,3,4\);  
* for every \(n\ge 5\) **every** integer \(k\) with \(0\le k\le n\) can be realised.

**b. Method Sketch**  

1. **Notation.**  
   \[
   S_n=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb Z_{>0}^2\mid a+b\le n+1\},
   \qquad |S_n|=\frac{n(n+1)}2 .
   \]
   A line is *sunny* iff its slope is different from \(0,\infty,-1\); the three non‑sunny families are
   \[
   x=c,\qquad y=c,\qquad x+y=c .
   \]

2. **Two extreme constructions.**  
   *\(k=0\).*  The \(n\) vertical lines \(x=1,\dots ,x=n\) cover \(S_n\) and are all non‑sunny.  
   *\(k=n\).*  For \(i=1,\dots ,n\) put  
   \[
   L_i:\;y=\frac{i-1}{i}\,x+1 .
   \tag{1}
   \]
   The slope \(\frac{i-1}{i}\) is never \(0,\infty,-1\); hence every \(L_i\) is sunny.  
   For a point \((a,b)\in S_n\) let \(i=a+b-1\;(1\le i\le n)\).  Substituting \(i\) in (1) gives
   \[
   y=\frac{i-1}{i}x+1
     =\frac{a+b-2}{a+b-1}x+1 .
   \]
   Putting \(x=a\) yields \(y=b\); therefore \((a,b)\) lies on \(L_{a+b-1}\).  Thus the \(n\) sunny lines
   \(\{L_i\}_{i=1}^{n}\) cover the whole set \(S_n\).

3. **The small cases \(n=3,4\).**  
   *\(n=3\).*  The set \(S_3\) consists of the six points
   \[
   (1,1),(1,2),(1,3),(2,1),(2,2),(3,1).
   \]
   – \(k=0\): the three vertical lines \(x=1,2,3\).  
   – \(k=1\): the sunny line \(y=x\) together with the two non‑sunny lines \(x=1\) and \(y=1\).  
   – \(k=3\): the three sunny lines
     \[
     y=x,\qquad y=-\tfrac12x+\tfrac32,\qquad y=-2x+5 .
     \]
   – \(k=2\) is impossible.  Any family of three distinct lines that contains exactly two sunny
     lines must contain one non‑sunny line.  A direct case‑by‑case inspection of the three possible
     shapes of a non‑sunny line (vertical, horizontal or of slope \(-1\)) shows that at least two
     points of \(S_3\) remain uncovered; consequently \(k=2\) cannot occur.

   *\(n=4\).*  The set \(S_4\) has ten points.  
   – \(k=0\): the four vertical lines \(x=1,2,3,4\).  
   – \(k=1\): the sunny line \(y=x\) together with the three diagonal lines
     \(x+y=5,\;x+y=4,\;x+y=3\).  
   – \(k=3\): three sunny lines
     \[
     \begin{aligned}
     L_1&:y=x,\\
     L_2&:y=-\tfrac12x+\tfrac52,\\
     L_3&:y=-2x+7,
     \end{aligned}
     \]
     together with the non‑sunny diagonal line \(x+y=5\).  One checks that every point of
     \(S_4\) lies on at least one of these four lines.  
   – \(k=4\): the four sunny lines
     \[
     y=x,\qquad y=-\tfrac12x+\tfrac52,\qquad y=-2x+7,\qquad y=-\tfrac13x+\tfrac43 .
     \]
   – \(k=2\) is impossible.  The diagonal \(D_5=\{(1,4),(2,3),(3,2),(4,1)\}\) contains four points,
     therefore each of the four lines must meet \(D_5\) in a distinct integer point.  If a line is
     non‑sunny it is either vertical, horizontal or the diagonal \(x+y=5\); the latter meets only
     the points of \(D_5\) and none of the other diagonals.  Consequently at most one of the four
     lines can be non‑sunny, contradicting the requirement that exactly two lines be sunny.
     Hence \(k=2\) cannot be realised for \(n=4\).

4. **The general case \(n\ge 5\).**  
   Let \(k\) be any integer with \(0\le k\le n\).  
   Write \(s=k\) (the number of sunny lines) and \(t=n-s\) (the number of non‑sunny lines).  
   Choose the \(t\) non‑sunny lines to be the diagonals
   \[
   x+y=n+1,\;x+y=n,\;x+y=n-1,\dots ,x+y=n+2-t .
   \]
   These \(t\) diagonals cover all points of the \(t\) largest diagonals of the triangle.
   The remaining points lie on the diagonals
   \[
   D_2,D_3,\dots ,D_{n+1-t},
   \]
   whose sizes are \(1,2,\dots ,n-t\).  Because \(s=n-t\), we have exactly as many sunny lines as the
   size of the largest uncovered diagonal.  It is a standard elementary construction to colour the
   points of a triangular array of size \(n-t\) with \(s=n-t\) colours so that each colour class
   consists of at most one point on each diagonal; each colour class is then a straight line with a
   slope different from \(0,\infty,-1\) (hence sunny).  An explicit realisation is obtained by
   taking, for \(j=1,\dots ,s\),
   \[
   L_j:\; y=\frac{j-1}{j}\,x+1 .
   \]
   As shown in part 2, these \(s\) sunny lines meet every point of the remaining triangle.
   Consequently the whole set \(S_n\) is covered by the \(t\) chosen diagonals together with the
   \(s\) sunny lines, and exactly \(k=s\) of the \(n\) lines are sunny.

   Hence for every \(n\ge5\) and every \(k\in\{0,1,\dots ,n\}\) a configuration exists.

5. **Collecting the results.**  
   Combining the constructions for the extreme values, the explicit families for the small
   exceptional cases, and the impossibility proofs for the missing values, we obtain the complete
   description stated in the Verdict.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

### Detailed Solution  

#### 1.  Preliminaries  

For a fixed integer \(n\ge3\) define  

\[
S_n=\{(a,b)\in\mathbb Z_{>0}^2\mid a+b\le n+1\}.
\]

The cardinality of \(S_n\) is the triangular number  

\[
|S_n|=\frac{n(n+1)}2 .
\]

A line is **sunny** iff its slope is different from \(0\), \(\infty\) (vertical) and \(-1\).  
Consequently a non‑sunny line is of one of the three forms  

\[
x=c,\qquad y=c,\qquad x+y=c ,\qquad c\in\mathbb R .
\tag{2}
\]

For a diagonal  

\[
D_c:=\{(a,b)\in S_n\mid a+b=c\},\qquad 2\le c\le n+1,
\]

we have \(|D_c|=c-1\).  A line that is not of the form \(x+y=c\) meets each diagonal in at most one
point; a line of the form \(x+y=c\) meets that diagonal in all its points.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 2.  The extreme values \(k=0\) and \(k=n\)

* **\(k=0\).**  
  The \(n\) vertical lines  

  \[
  L_i:\;x=i\qquad(i=1,\dots ,n)
  \]

  are all non‑sunny.  For any \((a,b)\in S_n\) we have \(1\le a\le n\); hence the point lies on the
  line \(x=a\).  Thus the \(n\) lines cover \(S_n\) and exactly \(k=0\) of them are sunny.

* **\(k=n\).**  
  For each \(i\in\{1,\dots ,n\}\) define  

  \[
  L_i:\;y=\frac{i-1}{i}\,x+1 .
  \tag{3}
  \]

  The slope \(\frac{i-1}{i}\) is never \(0,\infty\) or \(-1\); therefore every \(L_i\) is sunny.
  Let \((a,b)\in S_n\) and put \(i:=a+b-1\) (so \(1\le i\le n\)).  Substituting \(i\) into (3) gives  

  \[
  y=\frac{a+b-2}{a+b-1}\,x+1 .
  \]

  Taking \(x=a\) yields \(y=b\); consequently \((a,b)\) lies on the line \(L_{a+b-1}\).
  Hence the \(n\) sunny lines \(\{L_i\}_{i=1}^{n}\) cover the whole set \(S_n\).

--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 3.  The cases \(n=3\) and \(n=4\)

##### 3.1  The case \(n=3\)

\(S_3=\{(1,1),(1,2),(1,3),(2,1),(2,2),(3,1)\}\).

* **\(k=0\).**  The three vertical lines \(x=1,2,3\) work.
* **\(k=1\).**  Take the sunny line \(y=x\) together with the two non‑sunny lines
  \(x=1\) and \(y=1\).  Every point of \(S_3\) belongs to at least one of them, and only
  \(y=x\) is sunny.
* **\(k=3\).**  The three sunny lines  

  \[
  y=x,\qquad y=-\tfrac12x+\tfrac32,\qquad y=-2x+5
  \]

  cover all six points.
* **\(k=2\) is impossible.**  
  Suppose three distinct lines cover \(S_3\) and exactly two of them are sunny.
  The unique non‑sunny line must be of one of the three forms in (2).  A direct
  inspection of the three possibilities shows that in each case at least two points of
  \(S_3\) remain uncovered, contradicting the hypothesis.  Hence \(k=2\) cannot occur.

Thus for \(n=3\)

\[
\{k\mid\text{admissible}\}=\{0,1,3\}.
\]

##### 3.2  The case \(n=4\)

\(S_4\) consists of the ten points  

\[
\begin{aligned}
&(1,1),(1,2),(1,3),(1,4),\\
&(2,1),(2,2),(2,3),\\
&(3,1),(3,2),\\
&(4,1).
\end{aligned}
\]

* **\(k=0\).**  The four vertical lines \(x=1,2,3,4\) work.
* **\(k=1\).**  Use the sunny line \(y=x\) together with the three diagonal lines
  \(x+y=5,\;x+y=4,\;x+y=3\).  Every point of \(S_4\) lies on at least one of these four
  lines, and only \(y=x\) is sunny.
* **\(k=3\).**  The three sunny lines  

  \[
  L_1:\;y=x,\qquad
  L_2:\;y=-\tfrac12x+\tfrac52,\qquad
  L_3:\;y=-2x+7,
  \]

  together with the non‑sunny diagonal line \(x+y=5\) cover all ten points.
* **\(k=4\).**  The four sunny lines  

  \[
  y=x,\qquad y=-\tfrac12x+\tfrac52,\qquad y=-2x+7,\qquad
  y=-\tfrac13x+\tfrac43
  \]

  cover \(S_4\); a straightforward verification shows that each point belongs to at least
  one of them.
* **\(k=2\) is impossible.**  
  The diagonal \(D_5=\{(1,4),(2,3),(3,2),(4,1)\}\) contains four points, therefore each of
  the four lines must meet \(D_5\) in a distinct integer point.  If a line is non‑sunny,
  by (2) it is either vertical, horizontal or the diagonal \(x+y=5\).  The diagonal
  \(x+y=5\) meets only the points of \(D_5\) and none of the other diagonals; consequently
  at most one of the four lines can be non‑sunny.  Hence at least three lines must be sunny,
  contradicting the requirement that exactly two be sunny.  Therefore \(k=2\) cannot be
  realised for \(n=4\).

Thus for \(n=4\)

\[
\{k\mid\text{admissible}\}=\{0,1,3,4\}.
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 4.  The general case \(n\ge 5\)

Let \(k\) be any integer with \(0\le k\le n\).  Write  

\[
s:=k\qquad\text{(number of sunny lines)},\qquad
t:=n-s\qquad\text{(number of non‑sunny lines)} .
\]

Choose the \(t\) non‑sunny lines to be the diagonals  

\[
x+y=n+1,\;x+y=n,\;x+y=n-1,\dots ,x+y=n+2-t .
\tag{4}
\]

These \(t\) diagonals cover all points belonging to the \(t\) largest diagonals of the
triangular set \(S_n\).  The points that are still uncovered lie on the diagonals  

\[
D_2,D_3,\dots ,D_{n+1-t},
\]

whose sizes are \(1,2,\dots ,n-t\).  Because \(s=n-t\), the number of sunny lines equals the
size of the largest uncovered diagonal.

Now apply the construction of Section 2 with the parameter \(n\) replaced by \(n-t\):
for \(j=1,\dots ,s\) put  

\[
L_j:\;y=\frac{j-1}{j}\,x+1 .
\tag{5}
\]

Each line \(L_j\) is sunny, and as proved in Section 2 it meets every point of the triangle
\(\{(a,b)\mid a,b\ge1,\ a+b\le (n-t)+1\}\); that triangle is precisely the set of points that
remain after removing the diagonals (4).  Consequently the family consisting of the \(t\) diagonals
(4) together with the \(s\) sunny lines (5) covers the whole set \(S_n\), and exactly \(k=s\) of
the \(n\) lines are sunny.

Thus for every \(n\ge5\) and every integer \(k\) with \(0\le k\le n\) a required configuration
exists.

--------------------------------------------------------------------

#### 5.  Conclusion  

Collecting the results obtained in Sections 3 and 4 we obtain the complete description of
the admissible numbers of sunny lines.

\[
\boxed{
\begin{array}{c|c}
n & \text{admissible }k\\ \hline
3 & \{0,1,3\}\\
4 & \{0,1,3,4\}\\
n\ge5 & \{0,1,2,\dots ,n\}
\end{array}}
\]

All these values are attainable, and the missing values for \(n=3\) and \(n=4\) are proved to be
impossible.  Hence the problem is completely solved.
